paras: The threatened lynching of Joe Minor took place in December 1903, when laborers at a camp near Wellsville, Montgomery County, Missouri, were reported to have threatened to lynch Minor, a Black man accused of killing a fellow camp worker. Montgomery County's sheriff brought Minor back from St. Louis, where he had been arrested, and said he would protect him; no attempt on Minor is reported.

Bennie Ganson, known as "Slow Kid," was killed and robbed in a laborers' camp near Wellsville on a Monday night, about 7 December 1903. Minor was accused of the killing, and St. Louis police said he had admitted to the Fourth District police that he killed and robbed Ganson. Patrolmen Summers and Hunt arrested him on the morning of 9 December in a room at No. 812 North Twelfth street in St. Louis. Two other Black men in the room, Jake Darling and Clarence Suttfield, were also taken into custody; according to the report, they had been at the camp at the time of the killing and fled with Minor.

Sheriff Charles M. Wilson of Montgomery County arrived in St. Louis on the night of 9 December to take Minor to Wellsville to answer a murder charge. According to the St. Louis Republic, "it is said" that the other laborers in the camp were indignant over Ganson's death and had made threats to lynch Minor when he was brought to Wellsville. Wilson said he would be ready to give his prisoner "every protection" to prevent any such attempt.
The coverage does not report Minor's arrival at Wellsville, any gathering of a crowd, or what became of the charges against him, Darling, or Suttfield.

The episode appears in a single St. Louis Republic article of 10 December 1903, printed on page 2 under the headline "TO GUARD NEGRO PRISONER." Its subhead, "Montgomery Sheriff Comes for Minor, Who Confesses to Murder," presented the police account of a confession as fact, while the lynching threats were passed on as hearsay without comment. The article identified Minor, Darling, and Suttfield by race but gave no race for Ganson or the laborers who made the threats.
No other white newspaper and no Black newspaper in the coverage reported the case.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Joe Minor
bases: The only report says threats of lynching Minor on his return to Wellsville had been made by laborers in the camp, and the sheriff prepared to guard him (A1); no mob action is reported.

No one was killed: A1 reports only threats, made by indignant camp laborers, to lynch Minor in retaliation for the killing of Ganson, and the coverage shows no attempt. It is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.
Only one St. Louis Republic article (A1) reports the arrest and the threats; no other white or Black paper was found.
